angle: We thought we knew our ICP. Our closed-won data said otherwise
post_first_line: Our closed-won data disagreed with our ICP.
linkedin_post:
Our closed-won data disagreed with our ICP.

The gap between what we assumed and what the deals showed was bigger than I expected.

We assumed our ICP was pretty standard: a set of top segments and the types of businesses we sell into.

Then we looked back at our closed-won customers and went through the conversation intelligence transcripts. We weren't just reading for industry or size. We were looking for particular moments.

Product launches were one of them. When a company had a recent product launch, they were looking at Unify at a higher clip.

That's a trigger, not a firmographic. It doesn't show up in a list of segments, but it shows up in how buyers actually talk right before they buy.

Most teams define ICP once and never test it against what actually closed. The deals already tell you who is buying and when. You just have to go read them.

When did you last compare your ICP to closed-won?

lesson.title: Let closed-won data rewrite your ICP
takeaways: An ICP built on assumed segments can miss what actually drives deals.
Conversation transcripts from closed-won deals reveal moments that predict buying interest.
Triggers like a recent product launch can matter as much as who the company is.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last closed-won deals and scan their call transcripts. List the recurring moments or events buyers mention (launches, hires, changes) and check which ones your current ICP ignores.

angle: How to launch an automated outbound play without sending anything embarrassing
post_first_line: Delay every new outbound play by 20 minutes.
linkedin_post:
Delay every new outbound play by 20 minutes.

That one setting is how I keep automated outreach from sending something embarrassing.

Before anything goes live, I test the agents and snippets at a smaller scale. Then when the play launches at full volume, I delay the sequence. You can do that natively in Unify.

During the delay, I read through the sample emails and check accuracy. I'm looking for anything wacky.

If a reply comes in saying "we didn't launch this product" or "this is from months ago," I tweak the agent and keep testing.

Edge cases will still happen. We probably get one every few thousand emails. Based on the results, that's well worth it.

The goal isn't a perfect launch. It's catching the obvious mistakes before they reach thousands of inboxes.

What's your pre-launch check for automated outbound?
carousel: Slide 1: Automated outbound can embarrass you at scale.
Slide 2: Test your agents and snippets small before launching.
Slide 3: At launch, delay the sequence by 10 to 20 minutes.
Slide 4: Use that window to read the sample emails.
Slide 5: Check accuracy and look for anything wacky.
Slide 6: Bad replies mean tweak the agent and keep testing.
Slide 7: Expect an edge case every few thousand emails.
Slide 8: It's worth it. Catch the obvious mistakes first.

lesson.title: Launch automated outbound without embarrassing yourself
takeaways: Test agents and snippets at a smaller scale before full launch.
Delay the sequence 10 to 20 minutes at launch so you can review sample emails for accuracy.
Treat bad replies as feedback: tweak the agent and keep testing, and accept an occasional edge case.
lesson.exercise: Before your next outbound play goes live, add a 10 to 20 minute send delay. Use it to read 10 sample emails and check each factual claim.

angle: The boring first-party signal still booking 20+ meetings a month: someone sitting on your pricing page
post_first_line: 20+ meetings last month from one signal.
linkedin_post:
20+ meetings last month from one signal.

It wasn't a fancy AI trigger or a third-party intent feed. It was someone sitting on our pricing page.

We run other first-party signals alongside it:

- MQLs coming in from gated content
- People viewing our product tour
- CRM data, like closed lost opportunities segmented by loss reason

Everyone chases the new, exotic signal. Meanwhile the buyer already on your site, looking at what it costs, is the one worth calling first.

We run all of these inside Unify, but the point isn't the tooling. High intent on your own site beats most things you can buy.

angle: Our AI signal kept flagging pricing changes as 'major launches.' Here's the fix.
post_first_line: Pricing changes are not major launches.
linkedin_post:
Pricing changes are not major launches.

My AI signal kept treating them like they were, and it took me a while to see why.

I built a workflow to flag when companies ship something big. During early testing, it pulled in a lot of lighter stuff. Pricing changes. Internal tools. Internal hiring news. None of that is what we'd call a launch.

The problem wasn't the model. It was my prompt. I never defined what "major" meant.

So I rewrote it with specific criteria and structure. A major launch is one of these:

- A major feature
- A significant go-to-market shift
- A net new customer-facing product

And I told it to explicitly ignore things like pricing-only announcements.

If you don't define the category, the AI will guess. And its guess will be much broader than yours.

Tell it what counts, and tell it what doesn't.

What's the noisiest signal in your workflow right now?
carousel: Slide 1: My AI signal kept calling pricing changes major launches
Slide 2: Early testing pulled in pricing changes and internal tools
Slide 3: It also flagged internal hiring news as a launch
Slide 4: The model wasn't broken. My prompt was vague.
Slide 5: I never defined what 'major launch' actually meant
Slide 6: Fix: a major feature, GTM shift, or net new product
Slide 7: Then I told it to ignore pricing-only announcements
Slide 8: Define what counts. Then define what doesn't.

lesson.title: Define 'major' before you ask AI to find it
takeaways: Vague categories make AI pull in noise, so spell out what qualifies.
Exclusion rules matter as much as inclusion rules.
Early testing is where you catch what your prompt left undefined.
lesson.exercise: Pick one AI signal you rely on. Write 3 criteria for what qualifies and 3 things it should ignore, then rerun it on your last 20 results.

angle: The buying signals we watch when the real pain isn't public
post_first_line: Hiring lots of BDRs is a pipeline confession.
linkedin_post:
When I see a company hiring lots of BDRs, I read it as a pipeline confession.

Most teams never tell you their real pain, so you have to read it from the outside.

When a company is hiring heavily for the BD team, they probably need more pipeline. That's the first signal.

Then open the job description. It gives you a sense of their tech stack, which tells you about their current workflow and the potential pains you can go after.

Other signals I watch: headcount growth, and divestment in certain areas.

What this looks like will differ depending on the type of business. There's no single playbook.

But the pattern holds: a lot of this is external signals and inferring from there.

The pain usually isn't public. The behavior around it is.

Which external signal do you trust most?
carousel: Slide 1: The real pain is rarely public. Watch behavior instead.
Slide 2: Hiring a lot for the BD team? They likely need pipeline.
Slide 3: Open the job description. Don't just count the headcount.
Slide 4: JDs reveal tech stack, workflow, and potential pains.
Slide 5: Headcount growth is a signal worth tracking.
Slide 6: So is divestment in certain areas.
Slide 7: Signals look different for every type of business.
Slide 8: Infer from external signals, then tailor your outreach.

lesson.title: Reading buying signals when the pain isn't public
takeaways: Heavy BD hiring suggests a company probably needs more pipeline.
Job descriptions reveal tech stack, which hints at current workflow and potential pains.
Headcount growth and divestment are external signals you can infer from.
lesson.exercise: Pick five target accounts. For each, read one open job description and write down the tech stack mentioned and one pain it might imply. Use that in your next outreach.

angle: Spotting the signal is only half the job. The other half is the message
post_first_line: Intent outreach is half signal, half message.
linkedin_post:
Intent outreach is half signal, half message.
Most teams only automate one of them.

Quintin Smith made a point worth calling out: the power isn't just in taking signals and using them as intent triggers for specific plays.

It's also in the customization of the copy.

You get always-on monitoring for the trigger, and an action fires when it hits. Then that outreach gets personalized and made hyper relevant at scale.

No one has to look at an intent signal and then hand it to a seller to write the copy from scratch.

Both pieces are automated. Quintin called that really powerful, and it's easy to see why.

A signal with generic copy is still a generic email. Personalized copy with no trigger behind it is just guessing at timing.

You need both.

Which half of your intent motion is still manual?
carousel: Slide 1: Spotting the signal is only half the job.
Slide 2: The other half is the message you send.
Slide 3: Intent signals can trigger specific plays automatically.
Slide 4: Always-on monitoring means no one watches a dashboard.
Slide 5: Copy gets personalized at scale, not written one by one.
Slide 6: Sellers stop turning signals into emails by hand.
Slide 7: Generic copy wastes a good signal. Automate both halves.
Slide 8: Which half of your intent motion is still manual?

lesson.title: Automate the Signal and the Message
takeaways: Intent signals work best as triggers for specific plays, backed by always-on monitoring.
Personalizing the copy is as important as spotting the signal.
When both the trigger and the copy are automated, outreach can be hyper relevant at scale without manual seller work.
lesson.exercise: Pick one intent signal you track today. Write down what happens after it fires: who sees it, who writes the message, and how long it takes. Mark each manual step and decide which to automate first.
